events.summary: Country: Colombia Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. Entre enero y agosto de 2026, Colombia continuó enfrentando una crisis humanitaria marcada por la acumulación de impactos del conflicto armado y de eventos de origen natural recurrentes. La situación se agravó tras el terremoto de agosto , que incrementó las necesidades humanitarias en territorios que ya enfrentaban los efectos de la violencia, la pobreza y una limitada presencia institucional. Esta combinación de emergencias puso aún más presión sobre las capacidades de respuesta de las autoridades locales y nacionales. La intensificación de las hostilidades y el control territorial de grupos armados siguen deteriorando las condiciones de vida de comunidades rurales y étnicas. Los confinamientos, restricciones a la movilidad y limitaciones de acceso a bienes esenciales persisten como una de las afectaciones más críticas, incrementando riesgos de protección, inseguridad alimentaria y vulneración de derechos. El terremoto de magnitud 7,4 ocurrido en agosto evidenció la fragilidad de territorios ya vulnerables y donde las capacidades de respuesta locales ya enfrentaban desafíos y limitaciones. Más allá de la emergencia inmediata, el sismo incrementó las necesidades , mientras confirmó la urgencia de fortalecer la preparación, resiliencia comunitaria y capacidad de respuesta frente a crisis complejas y concurrentes. On 7 December 2025, renewed fighting in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, particularly in South Kivu Province, triggered a significant movement of people towards Rwanda. The initial influx was concentrated in Rusizi District, with asylum seekers arriving through border entry points and being received at the Nyarushishi Transit Centre and surrounding reception sites. The sudden increase in arrivals placed additional pressure on existing shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene, health, protection and basic assistance capacities The IFRC-DREF operation was launched on 16 December 2025 to support the Rwanda Red Cross Society in addressing the immediate humanitarian needs of people arriving from eastern DRC. While the initial operation was designed around an estimated 2,000 people, implementation took place in a context of continued population movement and evolving needs. During the four-month implementation period, the Rwanda Red Cross Society provided assistance through shelter and non-food items, health and first aid, WASH, Protection, Gender and Inclusion (PGI), and Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) activities. The response also focused on strengthening the capacity of volunteers to provide timely assistance and referrals at reception and transit locations. By the end of the operation on 30 April 2026, the Rwanda Red Cross Society had assisted 3,100 people . People in Gaza have few options to shelter from harsh weather. Some families have sought refuge in damaged buildings that could collapse around them. More durable shelter solutions are needed. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) is working with communities in Gaza on practical measures to help mitigate the impact of flooding. This includes the provision of sandbags to help prevent the tents of around 20,000 people, who have been displaced, from being swept away. The Zaatari Informal Market has played an important role in supporting refugee livelihoods, providing essential goods and services, and facilitating economic activity within the camp since its establishment. Emerging organically in response to refugees’ livelihood needs, the market developed into a central economic space along the main commercial streets of the camp, hosting a wide range of businesses operated by refugees. Yet, with close to one third of Syrian refugees having left Jordan to return to Syria since the change of government in Syria in December 2024, the population of Zaatari camp has shrunk from nearly 76,000 to around 43,0671 , affecting the overall camp economic activity. This analysis examines the evolution and transformation of the Zaatari Informal Market between December 2024 and June 2026, based on business tracking 2024 baseline data covering 1,507 surveyed shops, across three assessment rounds (December 2024 baseline, December 2025, and June 2026). By tracking changes in business status, sectoral composition, and ownership patterns, the analysis aims to provide insights into how the informal market has adapted to changing conditions, including business closures, restructuring, and mechanisms supporting continued commercial activity and shed light on the overall economic activity in the camp. events.summary: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday. That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election. events.title: Five key lessons from multi-hazard preparedness in Nigeria
events.summary: Country: Nigeria Source: ODI - Humanitarian Practice Network Olayinka Afolabi Nigeria does not lack information about humanitarian risk. Flood forecasts, conflict analysis, disease surveillance and community reports regularly identify where threats are increasing. The more salient question is whether that information changes what institutions do before people are affected. I confronted this question while serving as UNICEF’s technical focal point in support of government-led emergency preparedness processes. These included the 2021 Nigeria Countrywide Risk Analysis , its 2024 update , the National Contingency Plan and preparedness exercises in the Northwest. The analyses covered all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory and examined risks at local-government level. The national plan subsequently provided an overarching framework across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones, with State Emergency Management Agencies expected to adopt and adapt it. This was important progress. Yet our experience also showed that producing an analysis or plan is only the beginning. During preparedness work, the same questions kept returning. Who has authority to act on a warning? Which locations should be prioritised? How will state plans reach local government areas and communities? Are supplies available, and who can release them? What happens to agreed actions after a workshop ends? The lessons below come from supporting national and subnational institutions to answer these questions. They do not suggest that every gap has been resolved. They show how risk information can be moved closer to operational decisions, and where sustained leadership is still required. events.title: World: Evaluation of Disability Inclusion In EU-Funded Humanitarian Aid Operations, 2020-2025 - Final Report
events.summary: Country: World Source: European Commission Please refer to the attached file. Main Authors Zehra Kacapor-Dzihic Teresa Durand Catherine Chazaly Mariam Hamad Abstract This evaluation assessed DG ECHO’s approach to disability inclusion in EU-funded humanitarian aid operations worldwide during 2020-2025, following the publication of its 2019 Operational Guidance. It examined relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, sustainability and EU added value across both mainstreamed and disability-targeted assistance. Based on portfolio analysis, documentary review, stakeholder consultations and case studies in Jordan, Nigeria and Colombia, it found that DG ECHO’s guidance and programming requirements gave disability inclusion a defined place in humanitarian programming. DG ECHO’s sustained engagement also added value as attention and capacity declined in parts of the humanitarian system. However, operational application remained uneven, depending on partners’ expertise and access to technical support. In reviewed actions, accessibility adaptations and targeted support improved access for persons with disabilities, but barriers affecting different disability groups were not consistently addressed, and their participation in programme decisions remained limited. Monitoring documented reach more consistently than results, while continuity of support and local ownership were context-dependent. The evaluation recommends stronger implementation follow-up, practical learning and technical support, greater efforts to promote meaningful participation of persons with disabilities and their organisations, and more explicit sector-specific guidance.

events.title: Radiant Industries, Inc.; Special Nuclear Materials License Application for a Fuel Packing Facility; Environmental Assessment and Finding of No Significant Impact
events.summary: Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is issuing a finding of no significant impact (FONSI) and accompanying environmental assessment (EA) regarding the NRC's consideration of a license application from Radiant Industries, Inc. (Radiant). Radiant is requesting a special nuclear material license for a facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. If granted, the license would allow Radiant to receive tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) particle fuel for fueling the Kaleidos self-contained, 1-megawatt electric reactors. This phase of the planned operational activities would only include packaging TRISO compacts into monoliths. Based on the EA, the NRC staff has concluded that there will be no significant impacts to environmental resources from the requested license, and therefore, a FONSI is appropriate.
